Chapter 3: Rethinking God’s Role in Human Suffering
If you grew up believing in an all-powerful, all-loving God, dealing with suffering probably feels like a punch to the gut. I mean, if God is both good and in control, then why do terrible things happen—especially to people who haven’t done anything to deserve it?
It’s the kind of question that echoes in hospital hallways and sometimes explodes in moments of heartbreak. Honestly, it’s haunted people for centuries.
Picture a father watching his child struggle with illness. He’s torn between holding onto his faith and feeling angry. He wants to believe God is watching over his family, but every setback chips away at that belief. Those prayers that once brought him comfort—now they just seem to go unanswered. In the quiet of the night, he can’t help but wonder: is God ignoring his pain, or even causing it?
If you’ve faced tragedy, maybe you’ve wrestled with the same dilemma. Some folks try to protect their faith by insisting suffering must have a purpose—even if it’s a mystery. Others start to doubt, thinking, “How can I trust a God who’d allow this kind of pain?” Sometimes, the struggle to make sense of it all can feel as raw and painful as the loss itself.
But over time, something shifts. Instead of seeing God as the cause of suffering, some begin to see God as a source of strength right in the middle of it. What if God isn’t all-powerful in the way we imagine? What if God can’t prevent every tragedy?
It’s a different picture—not a distant, controlling force from childhood stories, but a presence that shares in our pain. A source of comfort and hope.
Think about a woman grieving the loss of her partner. She doesn’t find peace in the idea that her pain was planned. Instead, she feels less alone. She notices small kindnesses—a friend’s phone call, a smile from a stranger—and it starts to feel like something greater is at work. The God she comes to know isn’t pulling strings from afar, but walking beside her through the darkness.
This way of understanding doesn’t erase the pain, but it changes how it’s experienced. Instead of searching for reasons, people start looking for support. Instead of blaming God for what’s happened, there’s comfort in believing God is present in the struggle. The question shifts from “Why did this happen?” to “How can I find the strength to keep going?”
In this new perspective, faith isn’t about expecting to be protected from harm. It’s about finding the resilience to face it. The promise isn’t that suffering will be avoided, but that it can be endured. God’s presence is felt, not in the absence of pain, but in the courage to face it—and in the compassion of those who show up to help.
As people come to terms with this, they often realize their faith isn’t weaker—it’s actually deeper. It’s not about hoping nothing bad will ever happen, but knowing that, whatever comes, they won’t face it alone.
That’s a faith that survives—not because it explains suffering, but because it offers a way to live with it.
